column2: Tom, in his loud, flat Indiana voice, cheerfully comments aloud on how awful the Civil War and slavery must have been and how things might change after the Supreme Court's recent desegregation decision, on a bus that is still segregated. A skinny young man with a crew cut turns around with murderous hatred: “You damn yankees're all alike”, then “You damn yankees git ever'thin' wrong” and “An' it's the War Betwain the States, dummy!”. Every white eye on the bus fixed on them, none friendly; Rumaker shrinks and begs Tom to calm down; Tom, naive, tries a rational discussion, as if within the safe precincts of Black Mountain College. Consequences: Relief at getting off at the city limits in one piece; Rumaker feels like killing Tom for his naivete.

The next ride: a tractor-trailer loaded with frozen fish bound for Laurel, Mississippi; the driver, a small, nervous man with wavy black hair and a sharp Mediterranean face, hungry for company, talks mostly about his mother and gets along wonderfully with Tom.

After World War II, Olson often visits Pound, incarcerated for his naive pro-Fascist radio talks in Italy under Mussolini; it is through Pound's efforts that he meets Caresse Crosby. Consequences: The Olson–Crosby friendship.
More than twenty paintings by Willem in the American pavilion, with four other artists. More than 20 paintings

With the housemates gone to fetch crates of books, Pollock arrives in his Model A and drinks beers; nervous (according to one account he chases her around the house), Elaine phones the bookstore to hurry the men back; once back, they all horse around on the crumbling path behind the house; Pollock trips, Bill falls on him, and his ankle is broken. Words: Elaine's call to the bookstore to hurry the men back. Atmosphere: The muffled tension of being alone with a drunken man, then a carnivalesque relief that turns into an accident. Stakes: The two painters' rivalry turns a minor accident into a cause célèbre.

At dusk, Rumaker, his nose against the window, dreams of Gone with the Wind; Tom pontificates loudly about slavery, the Civil War, and the new Supreme Court decision; the passengers turn pale; a young man with a burr cut turns around, threatens them in a low voice, corrects the name of the war (“War Betwain the States, dummy!”); Tom tries a rational discussion, as at Black Mountain; Rumaker pleads and shrinks; finally the cord, getting off, relief. Words: “You damn yankees're all alike” — “You damn yankees git ever'thin' wrong” — “An' it's the War Betwain the States, dummy!” Atmosphere: Deadly tension beneath banal words; every white eye hostile. Stakes: Black Mountain's utopia confronted with the real South: physical danger for two innocents; the Civil War still very much alive.
Lectures and summer courses.
Lectures and studio courses at the University of Hawaii.
The Alberses give lectures and studio courses at the University of Hawaii

A former editor at the North Carolina Historical Review and a recent WAC (Women's Army Corps), she arrives in her gray Plymouth Cranbrook for the post of “administrative secretary”; she lasts only until December. Gray Plymouth Cranbrook Consequences: Departure in December 1954.

The two strays, looking for a big mother or big sister at the college, have tea and share simple meals at Betty's; she questions them about the college and often criticizes Olson, which makes Rumaker uneasy but provides a delicious irreverence. She and Tom swap army stories like old comrades. Olson, without saying anything, takes note of these visits. Consequences: Olson feels threatened with losing Tom and Rumaker.
Rumaker begins corresponding with Creeley several months after Creeley's return to Mallorca, from August 1954. Airmail Consequences: An apprenticeship that leads to the publication of “The Truck”

Asawa writes to the family friend Celia Sieverts that they have bought a sixty-year-old Victorian house and moved to 21 Saturn Street; they are gutting the interior to enlarge the rooms and let in the light. Albert Lanier takes on one job after another: a house for his parents, a renovation at a friend's, plumbing at home. A two-story house built in the 1890s, bought at an affordable price because the Victorian style was out of fashion; letter: “We have bought a sixty-year-old house” Consequences: The house becomes the main place where her sculptures are made and shown

A friend calls them: the city is tearing up a cobbled street to redo it; they spend the whole day gathering cobblestones instead of working on the house, exhausted the next day but happy. Next spring they plan to build a boundary wall with these stones and fill in to level the ground. Free cobblestones from a torn-up street, a boundary wall planned for the spring

A friend phones: the city is tearing up the cobblestones of a street to redo it. They abandon work on the house and spend the day gathering the stones. The next day, aches and pains, but happiness at the piled-up stones; a plan for a wall in the spring. Words: “Last week a friend called us up to gather cobblestones… we are so happy with the stones” Atmosphere: Joyful exhaustion, an ethic of salvage, work on the house interrupted Stakes: The house as a work of art in progress, made of salvage

Following Olson's advice to draw on his adolescence, Rumaker brings back to life a street gang from Camden, New Jersey, known around the mid-1940s. One cold night in late September, unable to sleep, he gets up in his underwear with pencil and paper, writes leaning over the top of the big pine desk, goes back to bed, gets up again; the draft is written almost entirely that first night. Late September, a cold night; underwear; pencil and paper; a big pine desk in the corner; the smell of mildew and gasoline from the abandoned truck Consequences: His first experience of writing as pure pleasure.
Olson's relationship with Betty Kaiser, a twenty-eight-year-old music student of Stefan Wolpe's, produces a son, Charles Peter. Betty Kaiser is 28

One cold night in late September, unable to sleep, Rumaker gets up in his underwear, writes standing, leaning over the pine desk, goes back to bed, gets up again, until the draft is almost complete at dawn. Atmosphere: Shivers, creative fever, the rediscovered smell of the abandoned truck Stakes: The birth of a writer

During the fall vacation of 1954, after Ellen has left the college, she meets Rumaker in Manhattan and takes him one evening to a program of Jewish folk dances at Cooper Union; he discovers the dances, notably the handkerchief dance, which remind him of Ellen dancing alone at BMC.

Rumaker reads his story in a low voice without daring to look up; laughter from Tom Field and Jerry Van de Wiele comes in the right places. Olson, enthusiastic, speaks of a “breakthrough,” likes the characters, especially Muskrat and Rosemary, the double outcast (Black and queer), the most decent of them all, and the clean way they are taken out of the story. He is viscerally astonished by the reform-school slang “brown eye.” He cuts the opening passage, judged “extraneous” (Rumaker will regret it), and concludes: the first thing he has written without a social message. Jorge Fick looks stunned, as if before a miracle. The slang “brown eye”; the opening passage cut Consequences: Rumaker at last feels he is on his way to becoming a writer.

Even before Creeley's letter, Olson announces at the afternoon tea given for Caresse Crosby (a rich Washington socialite of the Black Sun Press in Paris in the 1920s, an old friend met through Ezra Pound at St. Elizabeths) what Creeley thinks of “The Truck.” Crosby, recently in Greece with the World Community organization around a “One World” idea, is invited to visit the college and give a talk. Consequences: Rumaker learns of Creeley's reaction through Olson.
In October, Rumaker sends “The Truck” by airmail to Creeley and waits impatiently for his answer. Consequences: Creeley accepts the story for the Black Mountain Review

Olson invites his friend Caresse Crosby, back from Greece, where she works with World Community, to visit the college and talk to the students about this “One World” movement, as part of his Reading the Newspaper class, outdoors on the concrete terrace of the Studies Building. The class listens politely but without enthusiasm; an embarrassed silence when questions are invited. A clear, sunny day; apples falling from the trees onto the grass, picked up by Tom Field and Mary Fiore to eat, for pies and applesauce; an expensively tailored navy blue dress, 1920s bobbed hair, bright lipstick (an anomaly at makeup-free Black Mountain) Consequences: The talk fails; Olson tries to make up for it with attentions

On a damp, cold afternoon at the end of the October visit, Olson and Connie give a tea in their living room: cakes, real cups and saucers, a fire in the hearth. Caresse tells her anecdotes about Lawrence (paid in gold in 1928) and Hart Crane (locked up to finish The Bridge in 1930). Rumaker, sitting near her, is too intimidated to speak. Olson in an old rumpled seersucker as a jacket, a cord for a tie on a torn blue work shirt; Kate, two, takes her nap in another room; Connie serves the tea Consequences: There Olson announces Creeley's news

Olson, his hand on Rumaker's shoulder in front of the fireplace, waving a letter, announces that Creeley wants to publish “The Truck” in a coming issue of the Black Mountain Review. Rumaker, speechless with joy, keeps smiling at Charles's firelit face. Consequences: Rumaker's first real published story

Rumaker reads without looking up, expecting a flop; laughter from Tom and Jerry in the right places; Olson speaks of a breakthrough, raves about Rosemary and the slang “brown eye,” cuts the opening passage, concludes on the absence of a social message, and suggests sending it to Creeley for the Review; Jorge Fick stays openmouthed. Words: Olson: this is a breakthrough for Mike; “It's good enough for the Review. Let's try it out on Bob.” Atmosphere: A suspended silence, then enthusiasm Stakes: The long-awaited validation

A clear day; the students bring chairs out onto the concrete terrace; the small woman in an expensive navy blue dress, with bobbed hair and bright lipstick, sets out the One World ideal with gentleness and charm; at the invitation to ask questions, an embarrassed silence; Olson watches the faces, then multiplies his courteous attentions toward her Atmosphere: Bright sun, apples thumping onto the grass, polite unease Stakes: A clash between candid idealism and the college's hardened realism

A damp, cold afternoon; a fire, cakes, real cups; Rumaker sits near Caresse, speechless with admiration; Olson, in seersucker, plays the grand host, his arm moving from one shoulder to another, drawing from Caresse the story of Lawrence's gold (1928), then of Crane locked up (1930), while the dusk and the rain thicken on the windows Words: Olson finally announces, letter in hand, his hand on Rumaker's shoulder: Creeley will publish “The Truck” Atmosphere: The tense, awkward intimacy of students in a formal situation; the crackling fire; Rumaker unable to stop smiling at Olson's firelit face Stakes: The mythical past of the 1920s meets the present of a student in the making

Tom Hild, Terence Burns, and Rumaker organize Thanksgiving dinner for the whole community, so diminished that it fits in the lobby. Tom, a good cook, prepares most of it; the others bring the agreed dishes. Rumaker has cleaned and washed the second-floor windows with Tom, tactfully leaving Terence's door closed because of its barnyard smell; Terence is at the farm tending the rest of the livestock. A wood fire kept going in the big fieldstone fireplace; several turkeys roasting since dawn, creamed onions, homemade pies, red wine. Big fieldstone fireplaces; roast turkeys; creamed onions, homemade pies, red wine; tables and chairs borrowed from everywhere; wineglasses lent by Mary. Consequences: The last gathering in the college's old convivial spirit.

Rumaker stokes the fire and hears Wolpe grumble in his loose German as he vigorously pushes away the plate of hot peppers Tom holds out to him Words: Wolpe, in tipsy German, says he likes hot peppers very much, yes, but in the morning they burn his ass Atmosphere: Rustic frankness, Hilda smiling and humming

Wolpe tells, laughing heartily, how several of his Berlin mistresses of the 1920s, on discovering his betrayal, left in front of his door a pretty shoebox tied with a ribbon, filled in turn with their excrement and accompanied by a note signed by all of them Atmosphere: Frank laughter, a deeply lined face opening into the most wrinkled of smiles, Hilda blushing and complicit Stakes: Wolpe's openness, able to make fun of himself, which Rumaker, in hiding, secretly admires

The conversation turns to Marlene Dietrich and Jean Cocteau; Wolpe exclaims vehemently that they are insects to be crushed; Tom and Rumaker, who love Dietrich's 78s, are aghast Words: “They are bugs that should be stepped on!” Atmosphere: Amused, overwhelmed shock in Rumaker, who senses contempt for artifice and for queerness Stakes: The clash between Rumaker's gay camp and Wolpe's brutality

Rumaker comes into the kitchen; Olson sees him and shouts his praise, making scissor motions with his fingers Words: Every word is sharp, as if words were cut out of metal with shears Atmosphere: Rumaker blushes redder than the wine, a stronger intoxication than the alcohol Stakes: Olson's favor, precious and fragile

Made reckless by the wine, Rumaker, who has just reread “Maximus to himself” (a copy bought from Jonathan Williams), lightly puts his hand on the chest of Olson, who is leaning against the refrigerator, and tells him how open the poem is about him; Olson stiffens, draws himself up, and blasts him with a hard, haughty look; Rumaker withdraws his hand, steps back, and feels stupid Words: Olson snaps, to Wes more than to Rumaker, that Maximus is NOT him, is not about him, and why would people take it for him? Atmosphere: Sudden unease after an afternoon of bliss; Rumaker goes to ground, “the only sour note” of the day Stakes: The uncrossable limits of intimacy with Olson

Rumaker as Moonshine, barefoot, in a sheet toga, a barn lantern on his arm, little Kate's stuffed dog clutched to him; with no room to raise the lantern, he works the two children in the front row into the humor, casting theatrically disdainful glances at the kids standing almost on his bare toes Words: “This lanthorn doth the horned moon present; Myself the man i' the moon do seem to be…”; “This man, with lanthorn, dog, and bush of thorn” Atmosphere: A packed room, laughter from everyone except the two children, Kate's eyes fixed on her dog Stakes: Black Mountain's improvised magic, “making magic out of next to nothing”

The community's lowest point. After a long meeting, the college decides, despite its educational principles, to admit the mentally retarded son of a rich Southerner who hinted that he might then put money into the institution. The father was to announce his decision by flying over the college and tipping his wings in a certain way to say yes or no. For three or four days, everyone wanders the adjacent fields, noses in the air, listening for a plane that never comes. Three or four days watching the sky; never had such gifted men been assigned so absurd a task Consequences: The money does not come

At least one suicide attempt and threats of several others; another fire destroys almost all of Joe Fiore's paintings; so little money that almost no coal can be bought; it is cold, and pickup loads of wood burn up in the stoves in a single evening. A pickup truck loaded with wood, stoves devouring a load an evening Consequences: Just before Christmas, the community suspends all classes for three months; Creeley has already left (he will come back the following summer); about half of the remaining group leaves during the suspension; only eight to ten people remain.

A far more desperate appeal declares the situation critical and closing imminent; it opens with the sentence “This is the craziest sort of appeal,” which dismays many alumni. The first line of the communication: “This is the craziest sort of appeal.” Consequences: A tone displeasing to Forbes and the alumni.

During the 1954 winter vacation, Glenn takes Rumaker to a party in a Hoboken loft, where Manhattan artists were moving because of the cheap rents; Goodman, dressed as a workman, red-faced, a pipe between his broken, tobacco-stained teeth, laments having taken a young virgin that afternoon without lubricant and fears he hurt him, repeating his worries until Rumaker whispers to Glenn that Paul looks like a devil; later Goodman comes straight up to him and, without preamble: “So you think I'm a devil”; unsettled and annoyed at Glenn's betrayal, Rumaker leaves the party and goes back alone by bus to Manhattan, to Mary Ann Fretz's place on Minetta Lane in the Village. Pipe, broken teeth; cheap lofts; Mary Ann Fretz's apartment on Minetta Lane

Before the winter break, an exhibition of the correspondence received by the Crosbys in the 1920s and 1930s (Pound, Lawrence, Crane, Slater Brown) and of Black Sun Press books, including the first edition of The Bridge (1930). Carefully hung by the painting teacher Joe Fiore. Rumaker looks for tear stains on Crane's letters to Brown and finds none. The room where Tony Landreau weaves; the first large-format printing of The Bridge Consequences: Drawing attention to the college and perhaps a few students

Rumaker stays in the basement apartment of the composer Ben Weber on West 11th Street. He reads Hart Crane's selected letters and Philip Horton's biography, just out, devouring both to feed his hungry queer self. Looking for the tenement where Maxwell Bodenheim and his third wife were murdered, he happens to see Jorge Fick reading Crane's poems aloud to Pat Nelson and listens from a distance. First Avenue, Lower East Side; the two do not see him Consequences: Crane consecrated as a secret guide, against Olson's judgment

During the winter break, Rumaker, out looking for the building where Maxwell Bodenheim and his third wife had just been murdered, happens to see Jorge Fick in a tenement doorway not far from the Bodenheim apartment, reading Hart Crane's poems aloud to Pat Nelson, emphatically, with boyish enthusiasm and big gestures; she watches him with amused, seductive eyes. They do not see him; he listens from a distance. A tenement doorway, First Avenue; the recent murder of Maxwell Bodenheim and his third wife in the neighborhood. Consequences: Confirms a clandestine devotion to Crane despite Olson's disapproval.

Once again the faculty decides to close the college for the winter to save coal and electricity, an idea of Olson's borrowed from Antioch College (“at work in the field”). The finances are exhausted; the Black Mountain Review was supposed to attract students, without success. Huss and Olson announce that returning students will have to pay a few hundred dollars in fees for the next term; the work scholarships have disappeared, a major difficulty for Rumaker. A few hundred dollars in fees; savings on coal and utilities. Consequences: Rumaker leaves for New York; the question of the low-interest Bovingdon Fund, repayable about a year after graduation, suggested by Wes.

By letter, Ben Weber, knowing that Rumaker has no place to stay (Mary Ann and Seymour married and moved to a brownstone on 122nd Street), offers to share his bed until he finds work and lodging. Rumaker hesitates, knowing Ben's feelings, but accepts out of desperation and announces his arrival date. He leaves the college at dawn with his old battered suitcase (his mother's, kept because the new one had been stolen in Chattanooga), passing the Gatehouse, going down the mountain to the county road and then the highway toward Raleigh and U.S. 1 to hitchhike. 230 West 11th Street; a battered suitcase; departure at dawn; route via Raleigh, then U.S. 1.

One evening at dinner, Ben, blushing with shy pride, announces that he has won a Prix de Rome for a composition: he will fly to Italy for a week or two. He had said nothing in his letter, wanting the pleasure of announcing it in person; the timing suits Rumaker, who will look after the apartment (a series of recent burglaries on the block) while he looks for work and lodging. Ben is more nervous about his first flight to Europe than about the ceremony. Prix de Rome; one to two weeks in Italy; a series of break-ins in the neighborhood. Consequences: Rumaker stays alone in the apartment.

With a few shots of Carstairs and a few quarts of Schmidt's of Philadelphia, father and son are superficially amiable; the father's limp handshake and only comment: why doesn't he get a haircut. Despite midnight Mass in the little white church where Rumaker served as an altar boy, the pull of familiarity and of the refuge of home makes itself felt, even as, like Maximus, he becomes a stranger to what was most familiar to him; but the pull of Black Mountain persists. Carstairs (whiskey); quarts of Schmidt's of Philadelphia; midnight Mass in the little white church.

Rumaker spends Christmas with his family with the help of a few bottles of Carstairs and Schmidt's of Philadelphia; his father's limp handshake, his only remark: why doesn't he get a haircut; midnight Mass in the little white church where he was an altar boy; he feels the pull of home but leaves to hitchhike to Manhattan early in the morning after Christmas. A limp handshake; “Whyn't you get a haircut?”; Carstairs and quarts of Schmidt's of Philadelphia. Consequences: The decision to head back to New York and Black Mountain.

Hitchhiking, Rumaker is told by the driver, a young soldier, to get rid of a drunken Marine with a bandaged hand, from the same town as Rumaker; the Marine gets into a violent fight in front of a drugstore with three soldiers while Rumaker tries to call his father; he takes mental notes for future use, as with the dead bum on the bridge. Consequences: Material for the story “Exit 3.”

Sitting on a wooden bench at the massive table in Ben's kitchen, overlooking the garden of St. John's-in-the-Village, Rumaker tries out Faulkner's writing ritual (a finger of bourbon), an experiment not repeated, since alcohol dulls the imagination, and types the first draft of “Exit 3” on Ben's portable typewriter, lent to him, following Charles's advice to “write what you know,” after the success of “The Truck.” He works until New Year's while making the rounds of employment agencies. A portable typewriter; a glass or two of the fine wine from Ben's cellar. Consequences: A story begun; a writer's discipline resumed.

A holiday gift: a booklet of fierce satirical poems printed by Creeley himself in Majorca for the season, with a deep black cover, sent to his friends, a salutary counterpoint to Christmas sentimentality. Deep black cover; printed in Majorca.

Rumaker sends his mother a copy of the Black Mountain Review with “The Pipe” in it, a test and an assertion. She replies that she knows he can write a clean story if he really tries, not a dirty one, and asks why he does not write for the Saturday Evening Post (where his brother Bill works in the pressroom). Years later, his cousin Kay Hoffman tells Rumaker that his mother, who had given her the magazine to get it out of the house, had carefully cut out all the dirty words with a razor blade, in case the youngest, David, found the magazine hidden in the bottom drawer of her dresser. A razor blade; the bottom drawer of a dresser; the Saturday Evening Post
Two canvases bought by John Blair Lynn Goodwin, half brother of the sculptor David Hare.

After the shameful decision to admit the rich Southerner's retarded son, the college awaits the verdict: the father will fly over the campus and tip his wings in a certain way to say yes or no; for three or four days, men and women wander the fields, looking up, listening; the plane never comes. Words: Creeley: never had he seen such extraordinarily gifted men assigned to so extraordinarily absurd a task Atmosphere: Absurd, twilight, humiliated Stakes: The moral abdication of a college dying of hunger

Goodman, in workman's clothes, repeats his worry about having hurt a young virgin that afternoon; Rumaker whispers to Glenn that he looks like a devil; later Goodman comes straight up to him and lets drop his opening line; Rumaker, unsettled and annoyed at Glenn's betrayal, leaves alone by bus for Manhattan. Words: Goodman, without preamble: “So you think I'm a devil” Atmosphere: Chaotic, raw, smoky with pipe smoke; unease and betrayal. Stakes: An encounter with Goodman undiluted: total disinhibition before a Rumaker still in hiding.

Looking for the tenement of the Bodenheim murder, Rumaker sees Jorge reading Crane's poems aloud to Pat, emphatically, with boyish gesticulations; she listens, vaguely amused, her fresh, intelligent eyes on his; Rumaker stays at a distance, invisible, and listens Atmosphere: New York winter, chance, a secret interlude Stakes: The underground transmission of Crane, against Olson

Rumaker looks for the tenement of the Bodenheim murder, sees Jorge reading Crane's poems to Pat, stays at a distance, invisible, and listens Atmosphere: Jorge's emphasis and gesticulation, Pat's amused and seductive freshness, Rumaker a hidden spectator Stakes: Love for the banished poems, shared in secret far from Olson

Brought together by shots of Carstairs and quarts of Schmidt's, the father, after a limp handshake, comments only on his son's hair; then midnight Mass in the little white church of Rumaker's childhood Words: “Whyn't you get a haircut?” Atmosphere: A warm alcoholic haze, Christmas Eve sentimentality, the ambiguous pull of the family refuge Stakes: The wrench: becoming a stranger to what was most familiar, like Maximus

The appeal of December 15, 1954, brings in only about $250 and no loans; Olson writes to Nell Rice that no one even has money to buy food. About $250 collected Consequences: A worsening of the financial crisis that leads to the foreclosure

An essay defending nonabstract avant-garde artists: every vital style is a mode of thought; even the abstract artist always ends up with a subject; flatness is an illusion, like three-dimensional space; today's shocks are pseudo-shocks, and pastiche is king; some Abstract Expressionists are in fact Abstract Impressionists (Mitchell, Guston, Resnick, Francis), who keep the optical manner of Impressionism but leave out the scene. An implicit answer, without naming it, to Greenberg's “American-Type Painting” (1955), which had disparaged Bill as unable to tear himself away from the figure

Around the mid-1950s, the legendary Yankees first baseman Eddie Robinson asks to see her sports paintings; before the basketball and baseball pictures, disconcerted by nothing, he says: “I'll take these six”. No one had ever bought so many at once. She just liked his style, Elaine jokes. These paintings adorned the restaurant Robinson opened in Baltimore for years. Six paintings bought at once
Williams takes Rexroth's portrait; Rexroth claims his suit was given to him by Al Capone. A suit supposedly given by Al Capone; an unverifiable claim ('Yes? No?')
The few devoted teachers who have stayed on have received no salary for a year, and many have used up their personal savings. A year without salary Consequences: Tragicomic attempts at recovery

Olson tries to get state approval for the enrollment of Korean War veterans; the six remaining students run from one classroom to another, changing disguises every few minutes, to make the VA inspectors believe the community is flourishing. Six students; disguises changed every few minutes; VA inspectors Consequences: The ruse fails

The college agrees, despite its principles, to admit the mentally deficient son of a rich Southerner who hints at a contribution of money. The father is to fly over the college in a private plane and tip his wings in a certain way to signal his decision on a bequest. For several days, the members of the saving remnant wander the fields, noses to the sky, waiting for the sound of a plane that will never come. A private plane; tipped wings; several days watching the sky Consequences: Failure; closing in 1957

“Sound of Talking” appears in the summer 1955 issue: Purdy, with no connection at all to the real or mental geography of Black Mountain, no doubt gets his very first American publication there. Consequences: Proof of Creeley's openness beyond the circle.

The lower campus long abandoned, eight to ten people on site: rumor has it that Black Mountain has closed. A prospective buyer (wanting to make it a center for disturbed children) comes in person, finds no one, and has to inquire by mail; he is told that no, the college still exists and will go on existing.

A visitor arrives at night, climbs the mountain, sees a few lights, and finds two people drinking coffee, who kindly assure him that there are other people to meet in the morning; the ghost-town atmosphere makes him so nervous that he leaves by taxi at dawn. A few lights, coffee, a taxi at dawn

During the three-month suspension, members go to see the rich supporters of the past in person: the foundations refuse; the alumni are too few and too poor to give more than encouragement; many from the 1930s and 1940s are hostile to the Olson regime. Consequences: Nell Rice's mission to Stephen Forbes turns into a disaster: it leads not to funds but to foreclosure proceedings.

Huss and Olson seek to raise capital by selling part of the land and buildings; buyers come forward, but the consent of Forbes, holder of the first mortgage, is needed; urged on by Nell Rice, he refuses. Consequences: The college's financial strategy is blocked.

Forbes, rich and generous, cares little about the $5,000 still owed on his mortgage; he wants the whole property sold to pay all the debts: about $45,000 in back salaries to the teachers (who had accepted cuts to keep the college going) and some $40,000 owed to Paul Williams. He fears that a partial sale would finance operating costs and leave, at the end (which he considers imminent in any case), old debts plus new ones and almost no capital. $5,000 remaining on the first mortgage; ~$45,000 in back salaries; ~$40,000 owed to Paul Williams Consequences: He wants an honorable New England ending for the college.

Olson writes to Forbes that there are two responsibilities: the past debts and keeping the place open; “The College . . . matters to the society”, even if individuals do not always realize it; a good partial sale would honor both, a total sale would sacrifice one to the other. Olson's letter to Forbes Consequences: Forbes, fed tales of decadence and immorality by Nell Rice and others, no longer feels bound to anything but one thing: closing it properly.

After agreeing in April 1954 and again in April 1955 to postpone two mortgage payments, Forbes sets June 29 as the due date; in case of default, the entire balance becomes immediately due, hence foreclosure. Due date of June 29, 1955 Consequences: The threat of immediate foreclosure.

At the same time as the ultimatum, former teachers consider legal action for their back salaries; Nell Rice, Hazel Larsen, and Natasha Goldowski have written to the nineteen former faculty members concerned to rally them; almost all reply that they do not believe they have a claim and do not want to endanger the life of the college, while readily accepting repayment if no lawsuit or harm results. 19 former teachers contacted by mail Consequences: The lawsuit is put on hold.

Around 1955, tired (between the disorder of his personal life, the strain of keeping the college open, and the wish to get on with his own work), Olson calls his course “The Present”: before coming to class, everyone must have read The New York Times and the Asheville Citizen-Times; then Olson improvises. Prior reading of The New York Times and the Asheville Citizen-Times

Betty Kaiser arrives as a student to study voice and music; shortly afterward, she becomes Olson's companion while he is still married to Connie. Consequences: Charles's noisy nights in Betty's room above Rumaker's

For a Sunday community evening, a performed reading of Ibsen's Peer Gynt: Betty Kaiser as Solveig, Rumaker as the Button Molder; almost the whole college in the cast, a handful of spectators taken into the big circle; Wolpe writes piano music and special songs, including “Solveig's Song,” sung by Betty in a touching, delicately nuanced voice.

Work on Act V, scene 2 of Othello: Betty as Desdemona on a mattress laid on the gray-painted concrete floor, Rumaker as Othello; Wes has him place the pillow lightly over Betty's face; seized by the feeling of murder, Rumaker trembles, tears away the pillow, and breaks off the scene; Betty sits up, smiling, puzzled; Wes understands and has gotten what he wanted. A mattress on gray-painted concrete; the line 'Put out the light, and then put out the light'

Betty plays the mother and Rumaker her son Oswald in the last scenes of Ibsen's Ghosts; Wes suggests that Betty imagine the brain turning to mush; Rumaker, absorbed, stares at the stream through the window long after the scene has ended; turning around, he sees Betty and Wes looking at him, Wes with moist eyes, the only time Rumaker will see him visibly moved. Wes's advice about Oswald's hereditary syphilis; the stream visible through the window Consequences: Rumaker discovers by accident the Zen lesson of an effect obtained without seeking the effect

Rumaker hears Olson quietly climb the outside stairs, knock softly, then the springs of Betty's bed creak under Charles's colossal weight for nearly half an hour of repeated thrusts; he imagines headlines in the Asheville Citizen ('STUDENT KILLED BY AMOROUS TEACHER') and experiences it as overhearing his spiritual father's betrayal of Connie, whom he loves as a friend. Nearly half an hour; the noise stops as abruptly as it began Consequences: Rumaker realizes that his god has feet of clay; an awakening out of his Judeo-Christian erotophobia

A few months after the episode of the checks, Rumaker writes for the first time a story that Olson fully approves and that Creeley will publish in the Black Mountain Review. Three piles of manuscripts a foot high on the shelf of his studio after two years Consequences: The birth of Rumaker's own sound system as a writer

In summer, Rumaker and Tom spend a good part of their afternoons swimming in the rapids of the Snake River among the newts and snakes, sometimes dodging stones thrown by farm kids hidden in the bushes.

Charles, enthusiastic, urges his students to submit stories to a college competition at an arts festival at Greensboro College, then a women's college. All the manuscripts come back without the slightest honorable mention. On the manuscript of “The Pipe,” a single word in pencil: “Ugh” Consequences: Rumaker's first rejection outside the protected world of Black Mountain; Olson takes it with philosophical humor

On Olson's advice, Rumaker sends “The Pipe” to the New Mexico Quarterly, which also turns it down, making Rumaker doubt the class's enthusiasm. Consequences: Rumaker's doubts about the real worth of his story

One Saturday afternoon, Olson leads a crew to unclog a drain. Rumaker, depressed, refuses to take part and goes walking in the hills, guilty and nervous at having said no to Charles. Olson, amid the stench and the mud, reportedly said mockingly: “Rumaker can only write about this kind of stuff, eh? Doesn't want to get his hands in it.” Consequences: Reported to Rumaker by Wieners

After the marathon over “The Pipe,” Olson announces forcefully in class: “You are undoubtedly a throwback”, as if to explain Rumaker to himself. Consequences: Rumaker at first disconcerted, then: “So that explains it all!”

Wieners, 21, arrives from Boston solely to study with Olson, driven by his lover Dana, a volunteer fireman from Swampscott, Massachusetts. Dana has not said a word to John for the last hundred miles, teeth clenched, eyes fixed on the road. Consequences: John obsessed with the fear of losing Dana

Dana, ill at ease among the college's misfits and aiming for a conventional life (a coat-and-tie job), goes back to Boston to finish his studies. Years later he marries and has several children. Consequences: John's misery, but raw material for his poems; Rumaker sees it as a blessing in disguise

Olson's first assignment for Wieners, freshly graduated from Boston College: read “The Pipe” and write a critique of it. The text turns out to be snobbishly academic: Wieners accuses Rumaker of a hackneyed imitation of Southern writers, too influenced by Faulkner. Wieners wrongly believed that Rumaker was a Southerner and that the story was set in the South (it takes place in Gloucester County, New Jersey) Consequences: Olson tans his hide for his “misreadings” and tells him he must learn to read; Wieners submits and finds his master

Coming back from a movie in Asheville, Tom takes a shortcut; they come upon an overturned red convertible, its young driver thrown onto the road, covered in blood. Tom, a former army medic, rushes over and slaps the injured man's cheeks to revive him; another motorist goes off to find a telephone. The radio of the new convertible still softly playing country music; headlights lighting up the red clay ditch; smoke and steam escaping from the chassis; John shivers: the blond looks like Dana; sirens, state police squad cars, an ambulance to Asheville Consequences: John writes a poem that night and gives a copy to Rumaker; Rumaker will later see it as an omen of the end of the college

After Dana leaves, John urges two friends from Boston, the Dunns, newlyweds, to come and see the college; they settle at Mountain Stream and decide to stay. Consequences: Joe Dunn falls under Olson's spell and starts writing short, oblique poems

John and Carol being busy, Joe and Rumaker, with a dollar or two, walk down the mountain for a few bottles of ale. Joe talks nonstop about Olson's books and observations, hands flying in the dark. A few bottles of ale for a dollar or two; 3.2% ale; altitude 2,400 feet; past the Veterans Hospital on the dark, winding county road Consequences: A tense encounter with local baseball players

Five or six young players in dirty uniforms are drinking after their game. A wavy-haired blond, egged on by his buddies, comes over to Rumaker and Joe's table to ask for a light. His hands tremble against Rumaker's as he lights his cigarette; he mumbles a barely audible thanks and quickly goes back to his teammates, who congratulate him as if after a home run. A dead cigarette at the corner of his mouth; matches from a pack of Home Run cigarettes; the smell of game sweat; the mark of the cap band in his wet hair; a dusty baseball shirt with its tails hanging out; a barely audible “Obliged” Consequences: Rumaker, relieved and uneasy, suggests leaving; he looks over his shoulder at every pair of headlights on the way back

Rumaker, having bought baloney and a loaf of whole wheat bread, invites Wieners for sandwiches; Joe and Carol, starving, invite themselves. Having enough to feed only two people, Rumaker makes sandwiches for himself and John only; Joe and Carol, smoking, watch every bite. Cheap A&P baloney, whole wheat bread, a square oak kitchen table; John lives on black coffee and cigarettes Consequences: Rumaker vows never again to share his meager supplies with John, knowing he would invite three guests

After a few ales at Ma Peak's, the two men, free (Dana gone) and bound by their devotion to Olson, clumsily try to make love for a few minutes on John's bed, but give up: their attraction goes beyond the carnal, John's heart remaining in Swampscott with Dana. Consequences: John goes on pursuing his vigorous blond volunteer fireman; Rumaker looks for men who are strangers to him

The company does not understand the scene from Ibsen's Hedda Gabler in Wes Huss's morning theater class; Huss cancels the class until they do. Consequences: Wieners proposes staging Aria da Capo instead

After ales at Ma Peak's, the company walks back up and improvises a nighttime rehearsal around the grand piano moved down from the closed dining hall. The rehearsal degenerates into parody: the lines declaimed in Blanche DuBois's camp drawl. Rumaker, drunk but nervous, fears that Wes will hear their mockery. The Steinway grand moved from the now-closed dining hall

After the reading of “Exit 3” aloud to the community, Wieners, whispering so as not to be overheard, asks Rumaker whether he dares have two men kiss on the mouth, and read it aloud, with a smile of admiration tinged with hesitation. In the story, the drunken Marine kisses the hitchhiker Jim right on the mouth Consequences: Shortly afterward, Wieners begins openly bringing queer experience into his poems
Olson reacts in class with delighted surprise and quickness to Wieners's little poem beginning “Strange with women when / They find out you love men”. The poem will later appear in Ace of Pentacles.
Unable to hold out financially, Joe and Carol Dunn leave the college; John grows fond of Ed and Helene Dorn, and they of him, especially Helene.

Olson, Rumaker's graduation adviser, assigns him half a dozen essays on Shakespeare plays of his choice; Rumaker works on King Lear, Macbeth, Coriolanus, Timon of Athens, Pericles, Hamlet, Othello, Richard II, The Tempest, and The Winter's Tale. Olson adds that he should read the Greeks, especially Pausanias and Herodotus, and recommends Jane Harrison's Prolegomena (a copy in the library). A Cambridge Complete Shakespeare illustrated by Rockwell Kent, given in 1951 by Stephen, a learned workman at the next bench at Fischer Machine Works in Philadelphia; Onions's red-covered Shakespeare Glossary, suggested by Mary Fiore. Consequences: Only the word “meringuey” (about Othello) impresses Olson.
